verdict: Down again, and this week the bill came due at the top of the book: Alex Paige Moore resigned on 9/17 after twelve months — our longest-tenured client — and thirty-one minutes later the only thing anyone said in her chat was 'okay perfect thank you :)' about a bank account. Nobody has acknowledged her leaving. That makes six churned against thirteen live, and all thirteen are at_risk. follow_through is a flat 3.00 across all nineteen accounts for the second week running, with 662 commitments made, 267 kept and 369 lapsed; ownership_escalation (2.89) and disengagement_detection (2.84) are right behind it, which is the same sentence three ways: nothing is owned, so nothing gets closed, so nobody notices the client going quiet. The one genuinely new fact is that the security problem stopped being passive — on 9/17 Mica broadcast 'do not send your backup codes to anyone, including our team' and three hours forty-eight minutes later Mayson asked Sarah Lloyd for a code in the same chat.

team_broadcast:
Team — two changes effective immediately, both on me for not making them sooner.

FIRST, SECURITY. Nobody on this team asks a client for a password, a login or a 2FA/backup code in a group chat. Ever, no exceptions, no 'just this once because it's faster'. If we genuinely need access, Vivek arranges it privately. This week we sent clients an advisory telling them not to share codes with anyone 'including our team', and within four hours someone on this team asked a client for one in the same chat. That cannot happen again. Today, please go back through every client chat you're in — including the ones for clients who have left — and delete any message of ours containing a credential. Vivek is building the rotation list; if you know of an exposed login, send it to him directly.

SECOND, OWNERSHIP. Every account now has one named owner and the client will be told who it is. If you are the owner, two things are yours every week: a written update to the client with at least one real number in it, and an open-items list where every item gets closed in writing or gets an out-loud 'this isn't happening'. A promise that quietly expires is worse than a no — the client remembers it either way, and only one of those keeps their trust.

And a related rule: stop assigning work by @-tagging someone in a client chat and assuming it's handled. If you tag someone and they haven't answered within a working day, it's still yours. Across our whole book we've made 662 commitments and 369 of them died silently. Not one client has left because we said no to something. They've left because we said yes and then nothing happened.

Last thing. If a client says anything like 'this isn't sustainable', mentions leaving, goes quiet after complaining, or changes a password on us — that comes to me within the hour. Don't triage it, don't soften it, don't wait for the weekly. Two clients gave us that exact signal this month and both of them are gone.
pattern: We are fast and we are liked, and neither has ever been the problem. Median first-response times are minutes across the book — 43 minutes for Barbara, 14 for Vale, 7.4 for Sarah Lloyd — and clients pay early, refer friends and apologise to us. What we do not do is close. The failure is always the same shape: a commitment is made in a group chat by @-tagging someone, nothing makes that person the owner, the tagged person goes quiet, and the promise dies without anyone deciding it should. The client notices before we do — and then, critically, they stop asking. That is the actual churn signal on this roster, and it is invisible in every metric we currently watch: Vale stopped chasing $5,300, Lilia stopped raising three workstreams, Amber Haze stopped escalating after six attempts, Lauryn stopped asking about Facebook after 356 consecutive days, Alanna stopped asking us for anything at all. Every one of them then paid the next invoice on time. Compliance without expectation is what this book is full of, and it reads as health right up until the resignation message.
